title: Iona
hookLine: a Scottish community on an old monastic island: worship, justice and work together

cards: A small island off the west coast of Scotland, wind and sheep and white sand. Tradition says an Irish monk named Columba landed here and built a monastery, and that for a very long time the island was a place of prayer.
Much later, the old abbey stood roofless. Then a Glasgow minister named George MacLeod brought a strange crew out to the island: young ministers in training and out-of-work craftsmen.
They rebuilt the abbey together, eating, praying and carrying stone side by side. Out of that work came a community that still bears the island's name.

teach.b: The Iona Community isn't mainly people living on the island. Its members are scattered, living ordinary lives in cities and towns, and what holds them together is a shared rule. They keep daily prayer and Bible reading.
They account to one another for how they spend their money and their time. They meet. And they commit to work for justice and peace.
At Iona, prayer and politics aren't kept in separate rooms. The prayers there name wars, prisons, poverty and the earth. The conviction behind it reaches back to the prophets.
Amos hears God speak to a people whose festivals were full while the poor were crushed in the courts: "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols."

teach.h: LET JUDGMENT RUN DOWN AS WATERS.
teach.b: And then: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." Judgment there means justice, fair dealing in the courts. The worship was beautiful.

The problem was everything outside it. Micah puts it briefly: "what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" Christians weigh this differently.
Some keep the church well away from politics, wary that faith gets used by one party or another.
Others, like the Iona Community, hold that a prayer for peace that never touches how a city is run hasn't finished its sentence. Both want the gospel kept from being bent.
They draw the line in different places.

how: Members of the Iona Community live in their own towns and cities, keep a shared rule of daily prayer and Bible reading, account to one another for their use of money and time, and commit to action for justice and peace; visitors join worship and common life at the abbey on Iona.

games.q: you're in Amos's day. the festivals are full and the music is lovely, but the poor are crushed in the courts. what does God say through Amos?
o: take away the noise of thy songs; let judgment run down as waters.
games.why: the songs aren't the problem on their own. Amos asks for justice to flow alongside them: "let judgment run down as waters."

practice: Bring to mind one place far away where people are living through war or injustice, and hold it a while without rushing to fix it; then one place close to home, a street, a school, a courtroom, a shelter.
If you pray, hold both before God with Amos's words, let judgment run down as waters. If you don't, hold both with care, and ask what one small act of fairness is within your reach.

wordCard.voice: Iona. An island off Scotland, and a scattered Christian community that keeps worship and the work of justice together.

orig.note: Hebrew: justice, fair judgment. The word in Amos 5:24 the King James renders judgment.

carryVoice: Your line: prayer and politics. Justice, running down like water. Same time tomorrow.
